text:
In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the agency will require its officers to record vehicle stops with at least one body camera, Trump administration border czar Tom Homan said Sunday.

"They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action," Homan said on the "Fox & Friends Weekend" program.

Homan's comments come after federal immigration agents fatally shot two men six days apart during traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month. There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved in those incidents.

In a separate interview on CBS' "Face the Nation" show, Homan said money for the cameras was held up during the partial government shutdown earlier this year.

"The cameras have been purchased right now," Homan said. "They're training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide."

Traffic stops resume

The agency's tactics came under renewed public scrutiny in recent days after an ICE officer on July 13 killed a driver from Colombia in the coastal Maine town of Biddeford, about 15 miles (24 km) south of Portland. Six days earlier, another ICE officer in Houston fatally shot a Mexican national.

Homan said last week the agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures. Within 24 hours of Homan's comments, U.S. President Donald Trump directed federal immigration agents to resume them.

The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents' lack of body cameras.

ICE launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 and deployed cameras to officers in five cities: Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. The Trump administration moved last year to slow-walk the program, urging Congress to cut funding by 75%, Reuters reported in January.

In February, after the killing of two U.S. citizens during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota, then U.S. Department of Homeland Security chief Kristi Noem said the body camera program would be rolled out to ICE agents nationwide "as funding is available."

At least seven people have been shot dead during federal immigration enforcement operations since January 2025, when Trump launched mass deportations after returning to office following campaign promises of an immigration crackdown.

Affordable Care enrollment plummets in Kansas

The number of Kansans enrolled in an insurance plan available from the Affordable Care Act plummeted by 20% this year following the expiration of enhanced tax credits intended to offset premium costs.

New numbers released last month by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services show that enrollment in insurance plans available from the ACA in Kansas had fallen about 36,000 in February 2026 compared to a year earlier.

The data showed that 143,880 Kansans were enrolled in the ACA as of February 2026 compared to 179,920 in February 2025.

Data crunched by healthcare think tank KFF show that it’s the biggest numerical and percentage decrease for Kansas since the program started a decade ago.

KFF reported that the overall ACA marketplace enrollment fell 13% in a year, dropping to 19.2 million in February 2026 from a high of 22.1 million in 2025.

An analysis conducted by The Associated Press found that Ohio and Oklahoma each saw a more than 32% decline in ACA enrollment over the past year.

The AP reported that those states lost larger shares of their covered populations than any other state.

“Following closely behind, and losing more than a fourth of their enrollees, were Arizona, South Carolina, Minnesota, Indiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Louisiana and Missouri,” The AP reported.

The numbers just released at the end of June are different from the people who signed up for coverage by last January.

The new numbers reflect what’s known as “effectuated enrollment,” which describes the number of people who enrolled in coverage and also paid the premiums required for their coverage to take effect.

Last year, Kansas set a record for the number of people who signed up but didn’t necessarily pay the premium for an insurance plan available from the Affordable Care Act.

It was a 16.7% increase from the 171,376 who enrolled in the ACA in 2024 and almost 3.5 times the 57,013 who enrolled the first year the benefit was available in 2014.

But the record number of Kansans who enrolled last year was anticipated to recede with the expiration of the tax credits.

Five of the companies that provided insurance on the exchanges raised rates this year, anywhere from an average increase of 11.74% to an average increase of 33.4%.

According to KFF, expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits was estimated to increase premium payments by 114%, on average, for subsidized enrollees if they choose to stay in the same plan.

As a result, many were expected to drop their ACA coverage or maybe move to a less-expensive plan on the exchanges.

KFF has estimated that the enhanced premium tax credits saved subsidized enrollees an average of $705 a year in 2024, lowing their payment to $888.

Without the enhanced premium tax credits, annual premium payments in 2024 would have averaged $1,593, according to KFF.

“While the Trump administration attributes this drop in enrollment to their attempts to address fraud, this coverage loss happened at the same time millions of people faced steep increases in their premium payments — often in the double or even triple digits — with the expiration of enhanced tax credits,” wrote Cynthia Cox, senior vice president and director of the program on the ACA for KFF.

“While we do not yet know how many people have become uninsured, the ACA Marketplaces are often an option of last resort for people who do not have an affordable offer of coverage through their work and are ineligible for Medicare or Medicaid,” Cox wrote

The Department of Health and Human Services issued a report saying that growth in ACA enrollment was “improper” or “fraudulent” because individuals misstated their income to gain access to free plans.

“Media reports have focused narrowly on plan cancellations, a routine phenomenon that occurs primarily in the beginning of plan years as individuals are often auto-reenrolled into plans they may no longer want or need,” the HHS report said.

“Historically, 90-95 percent of enrollees who select an ACA Exchange plan during Open Enrollment ultimately effectuate coverage by paying their first premium,” the agency said.

“These reports largely ignore the broader landscape, including that an estimated 2.9 million improperly enrolled individuals have been removed due to various program integrity measures. In addition to the about 1.5 million enrollees CMS previously removed from subsidies, we estimate another 1.4 million either ended coverage or were blocked from coverage due to recent policy changes. Various policies and metrics point to these improper and phantom enrollments being pulled out of the system from late 2025 to early 2026.”

Constitutional amendment and immigration

Supporters of a constitutional amendment calling for the election of justices to the Kansas Supreme Court have introduced a new issue into the campaign: immigration.

A new ad hit the airwaves on Friday criticizing the court for “protecting illegal aliens” and warned that the state Supreme Court isn’t accountable to anyone until now. It told voters that on Aug. 4 they “can keep murderers like this off the street by voting yes on the ‘right to vote’ amendment.”

As of Saturday, the ad was targeted for Wichita and Topeka.

It’s not clear what murderers are being referenced in the ad.

The ad from the social welfare group Kansans for Democracy doesn’t go into details but cites a Topeka Capital-Journal story from March 3, 2020. That was the date the U.S. Supreme Court found that federal immigration law doesn’t override the state’s prosecution of identity theft.

Then-Kansas Attorney General Derek Schmidt had appealed a Kansas Supreme Court decision, which overturned three identity theft convictions because federal law preempted state prosecutions for using false or stolen personal information contained in federal immigration forms. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5-4 to reverse Kansas state Supreme Court.

“From the beginning of our country, criminal law enforcement has been primarily a responsibility of the states, and that remains true today,” Justice Samuel Alito wrote in the majority opinion.

“Our federal system would be turned upside down if we were to hold that federal criminal law pre-empts state law whenever they overlap,” Alito wrote.

“Indeed, in the vast majority of cases where federal and state laws overlap, allowing the states to prosecute is entirely consistent with federal interests.”

Three years earlier, the Kansas Supreme Court overturned the convictions of three men — Ramiro Garcia, Donaldo Morales and Guadalupe Ochoa-Lara — who could not legally work in the United States.

The three restaurant workers were convicted of identity theft and providing false information on state tax forms or private legal documents.

In a 5-2 ruling, the state Supreme Court concluded that federal immigration law prohibited Kansas from enforcing state criminal law because the information had also been submitted on a federal I-9 form used for employment verification.

The social welfare group financing the ad doesn’t have to disclose its donors under federal law. The group has booked or spent about $1.3 million on television and radio ads during the campaign, according to national ad tracker AdImpact.

Overall so far, an estimated $6.2 million has been spent or booked on broadcast ads for and against the amendment, according to AdImpact. The cost of the campaign is likely much more after campaign mailers, consultants and polling are counted.

Opponents of the amendment have spent about $3.8 million on television as they make a case that the amendment is an attempt to get around court decisions upholding the right to an abortion and provide more money for public education.

They say the amendment will put political donors in front of justices who will decide their cases.

Supporters of the amendment have spent or booked about $2.4 million, according to AdImpact.

Those numbers are fluid and can change as the campaign evolves.

Kansans for Democracy was incorporated by Brandon Smith, who was listed in public records with a Hutchinson address.

Smith is believed to be the former policy director for former Gov. Sam Brownback. He is now in private practice in Nashville, Tennessee.

Smith worked previously as chief of staff and assistant solicitor general for Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti, where he led multistate litigation and high-profile constitutional challenges.

He previously worked as executive director of legislative and regulatory affairs for former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin.

He also was deputy director of the Federalist Society and an adjunct professor at American University.

Skoog ready to get ads up on TV

Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog is about ready to get up on broadcast television in the Democratic primary for governor.

His campaign booked a small ad buy of $48,400 that is targeted for the Wichita and Hutchinson market only, according to national ad tracking service AdImpact. He has already spent about $8,100 on digital advertising.

Congressional fundraising

The state’s congressional incumbents will likely move into the general election with healthy campaign nest eggs compared to their Democratic and Republican challengers, new campaign finance reports show.

The state’s four members of Congress – Tracey Mann in the 1st District, Derek Schmidt in the 2nd District, Sharice Davids in the 3rd District and Ron Estes in the 4th District – each have more than $1 million in cash on hand for the quarter ending June 30.

Davids, the state’s lone Democrat in Congress, reported raising $656,845 in the second quarter.

She raised more than any of her Republican Kansas colleagues on Capitol Hill last quarter She had about $1.7 million in cash on hand at the end of the reporting period.

Davids has primary opposition from Sarah Preu, a technology and communications professional from Fairway.

Preu reported raising $17,439 during the last quarter and had $11,094 in cash on hand to combat an incumbent who keeps a large presence in the district.

Meanwhile, Democratic veterinarian and veteran Don Coover raised about $209,850 and had $241,518 in cash on hand.

In the first quarter, Coover reported raising $217,991 compared to $166,324 for Schmidt.

In the 1st Congressional District, Republican incumbent Tracey Mann raised $247,084 during the quarter and had $2.7 million on hand when the reporting period ended on June 30.

Democratic challenger Colin McRoberts, who teaches at the University of Kansas, raised $64,665 during the quarter and had $22,877 in cash on hand at the end of reporting period.

McRoberts has primary opposition from Lawrence attorney Lauren Reinhold, who reported raising $16,238 and had about $3,784 in the bank when the reporting period closed.

And in the 4th District, Republican incumbent Ron Estes reported raising $339,605 and had about $1.8 million in cash on hand at the end of the reporting period.

Democratic attorney Katy Tyndell reported raising $77,158 and had $103,984 in cash on hand as of June 30.

Tyndell is a founder of Leading Kansas, which she characterized as a nonpartisan civic engagement organization “dedicated to defending democratic institutions, protecting individual freedoms, and creating space for Kansans of all political backgrounds to find common ground.”

She now manages Tallgrass Management, overseeing operations and serving as legal adviser for affiliated family companies.

Meanwhile, Democrat Chris Carmichael reported raising $23,794 last quarter and had $16,343 in cash on hand.

Carmichael characterizes himself as a veteran who served for more than 31 years in the U.S. Army and Air Force, including over two years in Afghanistan.

He retired as a colonel and earned the Bronze Star for his leadership and service.

Lawyers announce support

for judicial amendment

Fifty-eight Kansas attorneys signed onto a statement last week supporting the constitutional amendment calling for the election of justices to the Supreme Court.

The signers include current and former Republican lawmakers, the Shawnee County district attorney, the general counsel to the secretary of state, the former head of the Kansas Chamber of Commerce and a member of former Gov. Sam Brownback’s administration.

“As attorneys, we recognize that this amendment would require our profession to relinquish a privilege that attorneys have held for decades, the ability to vote for attorney members of the Kansas Supreme Court Nominating Commission,” they said. “While we respect the commission and the attorneys who have faithfully served on it, we believe the time has come to place all Kansans on equal footing in the process of selecting the state’s highest court.

“Under the current system, attorneys are afforded a unique role in the judicial selection process that is not available to the general public. We believe every voter should have the same opportunity to participate in choosing the justices who interpret our laws and the Kansas Constitution,” they wrote.

The amendment would bring to an end a nine-member screening panel made up five lawyers elected by their peers and four other nonlawyers appointed by the governor.

It’s a process the state has used since 1958 when Kansans approved a constitutional amendment creating a special nominating commission for screening judicial candidates.

The system came about when former Kansas Gov. Fred Hall maneuvered to get himself appointed to the Supreme Court after leaving office in what is known as the “triple play.”

The controversy led voters to amend the constitution to install the current system.

Governor’s press secretary departs

You may know Grace Hoge and not even realize it.

Over the last couple of years, she’s been seen in many media photographs flanking Gov. Laura Kelly — often holding a recorder — as the governor addresses reporters.

She’s the one who gets to abruptly cut off reporters’ questions when she announces “last question.”

She’s also generally been on the front line of fielding reporters’ questions, regardless of how obscure they may seem. Her name has often been attached to quotes coming from the governor’s office.

And she was always responsive. It’s not that she gave reporters everything they wanted, but questions were generally answered — one way or another — by deadline.

Now, Hoge is leaving as the governor’s term winds down, and is taking an out-of-state campaign communications role.

“Serving as Gov. Kelly’s press secretary has been a deep honor,” she said in a brief email.

“I’m grateful for Gov. Kelly, my colleagues in the Governor’s Office, and the members of the press I’ve had the privilege of working with for the last three years,” she said.

Hoge became the press secretary in 2024 after working as communications coordinator for the governor.

She served as an intern in the governor’s office in the spring of 2023 and later had an intergovernmental affairs internship with the White House in the summer of 2023.

Kansas Chamber promotion

“I am deeply honored and humbled to step into the role of leading the Kansas Chamber’s advocacy efforts on behalf of businesses across our state,” Wilk said in a statement. “It is a privilege to represent the Kansas business community and I look forward to working with our members, state legislators, and Kansas’ next governor to make our state the best place in the nation to live, work, start and grow a business.”

Wilk’s experience in politics includes working as a campaign consultant for U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran’s reelection campaign in 2022.

Wilk earned a bachelor’s degree in strategic communications and a minor in business from the University of Kansas.

EMILYs List plays in Kansas House races

EMILYs List last week announced it was backing six Democratic candidates running for the House this fall, including five who are trying to flip Republican seats.

“This November, we have a real opportunity to break the Republican supermajority in the Kansas House of Representatives. EMILYs List is proud to stand with these bold women, and together give Kansans the leadership they deserve,” EMILYs List President Jessica Mackler said in a statement.

A group called the American Conservative Fund that is financed by sports wagering platforms has not only been running ads promoting the Republican candidates it favors in House races — it’s now on the offensive against their opponents.

title: When immigration status becomes a weapon; A Congolese national's search for elusive justice
description:
For migrants moving across borders in search of work, the journey from opportunity to vulnerability can be a short one.
Jean's decision cannot, by itself, prove that undocumented migrants generally avoid justice because of their immigration status.
It is not enough to ask whether migrant workers have rights.
Across the region, migrant workers may encounter low wages, delayed payments, wage theft and poor working conditions.
For migrant workers, these protections are particularly important because work and living conditions can overlap.
text:
When Jean, not his real name, a native of the Democratic Republic of Congo crossed into Kenya from Kampala, Uganda, through the Busia border in 2019, he believed he was travelling towards a new beginning.

He had been told there was work waiting for him in Nairobi as a tailor. With his skills, he expected to earn a living, support his family and build a future. But the journey did not unfold as promised.

Instead of Nairobi, Jean found himself in western Kenya, in unfamiliar surroundings and uncertain circumstances. The work he had been promised was not what he expected.

The place where he was taken to live offered little comfort. At one point, he recalls sleeping in a rat-infested house where rainwater came through the roof. He endured.

For migrants moving across borders in search of work, the journey from opportunity to vulnerability can be a short one.

Across Africa, established migration corridors connect people to employment opportunities in neighbouring countries and beyond.

The Uganda-Kenya corridor is one such route, facilitating the movement of people, goods, skills and labour across borders.

But for workers who cross without the right documentation, the search for opportunities can also become a journey into uncertainty.

For Jean, the absence of documentation would eventually shape how he viewed work, the police and his ability to seek justice.

“You are not Kenyan.” He heard those words repeatedly during moments of conflict.

To Jean, they became more than a reminder of his nationality. They became a reminder about the power he believed he lacked.

Years later, he would build a life in Kenya through tailoring. He would acquire land, establish a private business and support relatives across borders.

But before obtaining Kenyan identification documents in 2022, he lived with the uncertainty of being undocumented. That vulnerability became clear when he was exploited by people he trusted.

At one point, Jean was contracted by a pastor to make clothes for his wedding. The pastor paid part of the money upfront. But as the wedding day approached, he asked Jean to release the clothes before completing the payment, promising to settle the balance later.

Jean agreed. He says he trusted the pastor and believed that, as people of faith, they would honour their agreement.

But when Jean later went to collect the balance, he says the response was unexpected. “You are not Kenyan. You will not take me anywhere,” Jean recalls being told. The words unsettled him.

A similar situation unfolded with another client who was also preparing for a wedding. The client had not completed payment for the clothes, but with the wedding day approaching, Jean says he again released the garments, trusting that the outstanding balance would be paid later.

This time, when he returned to ask for the money, the disagreement turned violent. Jean says he was assaulted. Here reported the matter to the police.

The matter was eventually addressed, but Jean says he received only a fraction of the money involved. During the dispute, he recalls being told again that he was not Kenyan and could not take the matter anywhere.

The experience deepened a fear that had already begun to take root: that his status as a foreigner and, at the time, his lack of documentation could be used against him whenever he sought to enforce his rights.

For Jean, the issue was not simply the money he had lost. It was the message he says he repeatedly received: that because he was not Kenyan, his ability to demand justice was somehow limited.

“I thought, even if I am not Kenyan, I have no right to do anything here,” he recalls.

That fear would later resurface in his own tailoring business.

Jean had invested in fabric, including ‘kitenge’, and employed a young man to help him sell the stock. When Jean travelled to Kampala to restock his business, he says the employee sold some of the material but failed to account for the money.

When Jean confronted him, he says he was once again told that he was not Kenyan and could not take the matter anywhere. This time, Jean went to the police again.

The employee was arrested and some of the missing fabric was recovered. Jean was given the option of pursuing the matter in court. He chose not to.

“Life is like this,” he said.

Jean's decision cannot, by itself, prove that undocumented migrants generally avoid justice because of their immigration status.

But it illustrates a deeper question: what happens when people who may be vulnerable to exploitation do not feel safe enough to report it?

The difficulty of finding migrants willing to speak publicly became part of this investigation.

Several undocumented migrants approached for this story declined to be interviewed on the record, citing fears of arrest, deportation or retaliation.

Their silence cannot be treated as proof of abuse, but raises a question that extends beyond whether migrants have rights on paper: what happens when the people most vulnerable to exploitation are also the least able to report it?

For people living with uncertainty over their immigration status, seeking help can carry its own psychological burden. A police station, immigration office or other authority may appear less like a source of protection and more like a potential threat.

Matthew Mbuvi, a psychological first-aid practitioner, says people who have experienced displacement, violence, exploitation or prolonged insecurity may first need safety, empathy and practical support before they are able to navigate complex systems or seek redress.

“Psychological first aid is the first human, practical support that you can give to someone who is in distress,” says Mbuvi.

He says such support may involve listening without judgement, helping a person access immediate basic needs and linking them to appropriate services, including documentation and legal support.

“It is important to try to get into their shoes,” he says. “Try to empathise with their situation so that you are able to understand what they are going through.”

For migrants who have experienced prolonged insecurity, reporting abuse may therefore involve more than overcoming a legal barrier. It may also require overcoming fear.

That gap between rights on paper and access to justice in practice is at the heart of the experience of many migrant workers, says Elijah Rottok, an advocate and Senior Human Rights Officer at the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights.

According to Rottok, undocumented status does not erase a person's fundamental rights.

Kenya's Constitution protects the rights of “every person,” not only citizens. Article 29 protects individuals from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Article 47 guarantees the right to fair administrative action, while Article 50 provides the right to a fair trial.

“For workers, Article 41 guarantees the right to fair labour practices, reasonable working conditions and fair remuneration,”Rottok adds.

In principle, therefore, a worker's immigration status should not give an employer permission to exploit them or deny them payment for work already performed. But Rottok says the reality can be very different.

“Complaints received by human rights organisations commonly involve wage theft, confiscation of identity documents, physical assault, psychological abuse and extortion.”

In cases of wage theft, he says, employers may threaten to report workers to immigration authorities rather than address the labour dispute.

The result, he argues, is a climate in which immigration status can become a tool of control.

A worker who has not been paid may hesitate to complain. A person who has been assaulted may fear approaching the police. A migrant whose documents have been confiscated may worry that seeking help could lead to arrest or deportation.

The vulnerability, Rottok argues, is structural.

When migrants lack documentation, they may be pushed further into informal employment, where labour protections can be difficult to enforce. Fear of authorities can make reporting abuse harder, while those who exploit workers may operate with a sense of impunity. The scale of the problem is also difficult to establish.

Kenya has no reliable official figure for the number of undocumented migrants living and working in the country. That absence of data makes it difficult to measure the full extent of their vulnerability or determine how many may be unable or unwilling to report exploitation.

Jean's experience unfolds within that wider uncertainty.

A 2025 International Labour Organization (ILO) assessment examining access to complaints and remedies for migrant workers in Kenya and Uganda identified gaps in the legal and institutional systems intended to protect migrant workers and provide avenues for redress.

The findings raise a question that extends beyond Jean's experience. It is not enough to ask whether migrant workers have rights.

The deeper question is whether they know those rights, trust the institutions responsible for protecting them and feel safe enough to use them.

For Jean, the law may have existed on paper. But for a long time, he did not believe it belonged to him.

His story also reveals another side of migration — one often missing from conversations focused on borders, immigration status and enforcement.

Jean is not only a migrant who once faced vulnerability. He is a skilled tailor, an entrepreneur, an employer and an economic contributor.

Through his business, he has sold clothes, employed others, bought land and supported relatives across borders.

Every month, he sends money to family members. Some live in Uganda, while others remain in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

His journey reflects what migration experts describe as the migration-development nexus.

Migration is often discussed through statistics: the number of people crossing borders, the number of migrants without documents or the number of workers moving from one country to another.

But migration also involves skills, businesses, family networks and financial support.

Jean's tailoring skills have allowed him to create an economic life in Kenya. At the same time, his earnings support people beyond Kenya's borders. This is the less visible side of labour migration.

Yet the same systems that enable people to move in search of work can also expose them to exploitation.

Across the region, migrant workers may encounter low wages, delayed payments, wage theft and poor working conditions. In some sectors, they may also face discrimination based on nationality.

The ILO's decent work framework emphasises rights at work, fair remuneration, safe working conditions, non-discrimination and social protection.

For migrant workers, these protections are particularly important because work and living conditions can overlap.

Domestic workers, for example, may live in the same places where they work. In other sectors, workers may depend heavily on an employer for accommodation, food or transport. That dependence can make it harder to leave abusive situations.

Jean's own journey began with information passed from one person to another. He was promised work in Nairobi.

The reality he encountered was different. But today, he is no longer the young man who arrived uncertain of where he would sleep or whether the work he had been promised would exist.

His sewing machine, his fabric and his business represent more than income. They are evidence of a migrant who has created value despite the insecurity surrounding his early years in Kenya.

He has since moved from western Kenya to the Rift Valley, where he continues to run his business. A move he once feared when he was undocumented is now part of his life. He also visits his family in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

His journey complicates the way migrants are often portrayed. They are not simply victims or statistics. They are workers. They are entrepreneurs. They are employers. They support families and contribute to local economies. They also have rights.

For Jean, documentation eventually brought a greater sense of security.

But his experience raises a larger question: should protection from exploitation depend on whether a worker possesses the right papers?

Kenya's Constitution says fundamental rights belong to every person. Yet many migrants continue to live as though those rights are conditional.

For Jean, the needle has always been a tool of survival.

text:
A man fatally hit by a truck in Florida while running from an encounter with immigration agents was visiting from Mexico, according to a nonprofit organization supporting his widow.

A spokeswoman for the organization identified the man as Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, 28, of Guanajuato State.

State and federal officials have repeatedly declined to identify the man who was killed last Tuesday when he ran on to a busy roadway and was struck by a tractor-trailer. The man was fleeing an encounter with agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations at a Wawa gas station in St. Augustine, Fla.

The nonprofit, Colectivo Árbol, which supports farmworkers in Central Florida, is hosting the man’s wife, who arrived from Mexico on Friday to claim his body, said the group’s spokeswoman, Isaret Jeffers.

Ms. Jeffers said that, according to Mr. Coronilla’s wife, he was visiting on a valid tourist visa and had planned to return to his home country on Saturday. The New York Times could not independently verify the claim.

Homeland Security officials did not respond to questions on Saturday about Mr. Coronilla’s visa status or the circumstances that preceded his death.

Mr. Coronilla died shortly after ICE agents, in two unrelated instances, shot and killed immigrants during attempted traffic stops in Houston and Biddeford, Maine. The deaths have again heightened scrutiny on ICE tactics amid an escalation of President Trump’s campaign to detain and deport immigrants.

The Department of Homeland Security officials have cast the two shootings as cases of self-defense; no video footage of the shootings has emerged so far. The officials have also said little about what unfolded at the Wawa in St. Augustine.

Mr. Coronilla and three others had been in a vehicle at the gas station, a highway patrol spokesman said last week. The whereabouts of the other three people remain unknown.

Ms. Jeffers said that, according to Mr. Coronilla’s wife, her husband had been in the United States for three weeks with friends, first in Georgia and then in Florida, but just for a couple of days.

Mr. Coronilla ran a restaurant in his hometown, San Luis de la Paz, Ms. Jeffers said. “He didn’t want to stay in the United States,” she said. “He didn’t want to leave his children.”

A motorist who rendered aid to Mr. Coronilla told The New York Times that she saw a uniformed St. Johns County deputy in his marked patrol car pursuing the man as he ran on the busy road in front of the gas station. A St. Johns County police spokeswoman on Friday did not respond to questions about whether a deputy was involved in the incident.

Sara Atkinson, 42, said Mr. Coronilla ran past her car as she was turning before the truck plowed into him in the opposite lanes. He appeared to be fleeing toward a wooded area, she said.

Ms. Atkinson, a veterinarian nurse, said she pulled over and rushed to the man, who was gasping for air under the truck. She said she frantically tried chest compressions, urging him to keep fighting, before paramedics arrived and he succumbed to his injuries.

“I want his family to know he didn’t die alone,” Ms. Atkinson said through tears. “I was with him.”

text:
The vigil on Canal Street has grown every night since 7 July. It began when two neighbors nailed white roses to a utility pole. Within hours, streams of people brought candles and carnations. By the seventh night, the sidewalk was enveloped by votive candles painted with the Virgin of Guadalupe, Mexican flags flapping alongside Texas ones, and a wooden cross ringed with photographs of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old husband and father who was shot and killed by ICE on this corner of Houston’s Magnolia Park neighborhood.

“Magnolia Park is a tight-knit community. Neighbors know each other and they help each other,” said JoAnna Rodriguez, co-founder of the non-profit Magnolia Park Arts and Community, housed two blocks away from the site of the shooting. “So when we heard what had happened, our first reaction was, ‘Who was it?’”

Salgado Araujo, who employed more than a dozen workers building homes across the region, was driving to work with three others when he was killed by federal immigration agents on 7 July. He was not the man immigration officers said they were looking for.

“It could have been anybody,” said Jesse E Rodriguez, JoAnna’s husband and an artist who has lived in the neighborhood his whole life. “It could have been me or a sibling. My little brother buys breakfast right there before he goes to work,” he said, pointing to a shop across the street.

The killing has landed in a neighborhood defined by more than a century of arrival and endurance. Once called Houston’s “Little Mexico”, Magnolia Park took shape in the early 1900s as Mexican families settled along the channel to build the docks and refineries that made the city rich, followed by thousands more fleeing the Mexican Revolution. But in recent years, the neighborhood has started to change: century-old homes are increasingly sold off to developers, rents are climbing without any matching investment in the community and longtime families watch the block they grew up on grow less familiar by the year. All the while, the neighborhood grapples with the long shadow of police violence.

The fatal shooting of Salgado Araujo has only further shaken that uneasy ground, leaving residents wary of unmarked cars, reluctant to leave home before sunrise and uncertain whether anyone is safe from being mistaken for someone else.

But the fear has curdled into something else too: anger – and a determination that has pulled neighbors into a shared fight.

Ten days after Salgado Araujo’s death, longtime residents are trading phone numbers, watching each other’s blocks and packing city hall by the hundreds, insisting that the loss of one man become the reason the rest of them look out for one another, in a neighborhood that has always had to look out for itself.

“We feel it on a level we can’t even describe,” said a neighbor who declined to share his name for fear of retaliation. “Everybody knows that what happened is wrong. How will we not stand with our people, stand behind them, especially when something so vicious and ugly happened?”

A neighborhood changing

To understand why the killing landed with such force in Magnolia Park, residents said, requires understanding how the neighborhood came to be Latino in the first place – and why it has stayed that way for more than a century.

Jose Aranda, who teaches Mexican American literature at Rice University and grew up in Magnolia Park, traces the area’s identity to Houston’s economic geography. The city’s rise as a shipping and oil hub – after the deadliest storm in US history swept through the area and an erupting gusher launched Texas’ oil boom at the turn of the 20th century – created enormous demand for labor along the Houston ship channel. Mexican workers were recruited in growing numbers to work the docks, warehouses and refineries lining the boulevards that still run parallel to Canal Street today.

“This is why people continue to immigrate to these neighborhoods,” Aranda said. “They’re low-cost neighborhoods, but they’re also situated economically in the places that Houston is most strong economically.”

Adela Cedillo, a historian at the University of Houston who has lived in East End for 15 years, said the community’s Mexican and Mexican American character solidified as earlier waves of German and Chinese immigrants moved out of the neighborhood over the past century. Salvadorans arrived after their country’s civil war. More recently, Guatemalans and Hondurans have added to the mix. But the Tejano core, the Mexican American families who trace their Texas roots back generations, has anchored the area, which residents call a barrio to highlight this history and as a point of pride.

It’s a place where someone won’t be looked down upon for speaking Spanish, and where residents are proud to play their music or splash around the swimming pool at Mason Park. It’s where Catholic, Protestant and Evangelical churches have provided spiritual guidance, and the small businesses owned by Mexican immigrants, including bakeries and restaurants, line the streets. “There’s always a quinceañera. There’s always a boda,” said Aranda. “Life happens here, and that sense of community makes joy feel safe.”

But the neighborhood has been changing, a familiar phenomenon in most major urban centers. Century-old homes, many built by the same immigrant families whose descendants still live there, have increasingly been sold to developers who demolish them and erect town homes costing half a million dollars or more.

“Houston has this reputation that anything that’s built can be easily unbuilt, destroyed,” said Aranda. “It’s very hard to hold on to historic homes and buildings because it’s always been a developer’s landscape. They control the politics.”

Cedillo said she has watched rents climb steadily even as services and infrastructure lag behind. Between 2018 and 2023, Magnolia Park’s Hispanic population shrank by 15%, despite the increase in new housing.

“Many of us whose families have been here for generations are still here, but some of us have left,” said Jesse E Rodriguez. “I tell the friends that left, ‘Hey, you need to come back to where you come from. These streets made you who you are.’”

A long history of police violence

Racial tensions between authorities and the Magnolia Park community are not new.

In 1977, Joe Campos Torres, a 23-year-old Vietnam war veteran, was beaten by Houston police officers and drowned in the Buffalo Bayou, not far from where Salgado Araujo was killed. The officers involved received only probation, a sentence so light it sparked the Moody Park riot the following year, when simmering tension boiled over into a violent clash between residents and police officers.

“Whether it’s Joe Campos Torres at 23 or Araujo at 52, it’s just senseless and so damaging to everybody,” Aranda said.

He added that growing up in Magnolia Park meant absorbing, without ever being explicitly taught, a wariness toward law enforcement passed down through generations. “You needed to be always strait-laced,” he said. “You cannot really mess around with them because there was a way that barrios were intensely patrolled, and we just didn’t have any faith that law enforcement would follow the rules.”

Cedillo said the community’s collective memory of Campos Torres’ killing shaped how quickly and viscerally residents responded to Salgado Araujo’s. “These stories are marked by segregation, racial profiling, police harassment,” she said.

That backdrop has fed a swirl of anxious speculation about a separate, unrelated phenomenon: a string of bodies recovered from Buffalo Bayou in recent years. Cedillo said residents have begun to connect these deaths, however loosely, to the current climate of fear, even circulating theories involving a serial killer or a deliberate campaign against Latino residents. She stopped short of endorsing those theories but said the vacuum of information from authorities had allowed them to flourish.

“If an unmarked vehicle is trying to pull me over off the road, and especially if there are men with masks, I’m not gonna stop,” said JoAnna Rodriguez, referring to how the ICE agents tailed Salgado Araujo’s vehicle. “I would think they’re trying to rob me, or that I’m probably the next victim that’s gonna be thrown into the bayou.”

Keeping the barrio together

For all that has changed on Canal Street, what residents describe as most durable is each other. At a public viewing held Thursday at a funeral home in East End, hundreds of mourners who had never met Salgado Araujo filed past his casket for hours. His sons, 29-year-old Ronaldo and 27-year-old Lorenzo Jr, stood beside the casket the entire evening.

Activists are vowing to get justice for Salgado Araujo by calling for accountability and an independent investigation of the killing. They’re rallying at city hall and holding more “know your rights” trainings. They’re also bringing the broader Houston community together with protests that feature art for healing.

Throughout the day, neighbors continue to gather where Salgado Araujo died, lighting candles, playing music, trading phone numbers so they can check on one another. It is the same impulse, Cedillo said, that has always defined the neighborhood, whether the threat came from a squad car in 1977 or an unmarked SUV in 2026.

“We’re not asking for much,” she said. “We just want to be treated like humans, with due process and within the framework of the rule of law.”

text:
PORTLAND – Over 500 protesters gathered in the rain in Monument Square on Saturday afternoon, five days after a federal immigration officer shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian immigrant, in Biddeford. Guerrero’s death on Monday was the second fatal shooting at the hands of an ICE agent in the U.S. in less than a week.

The protest was organized by the Maine Party for Socialism and Liberation, part of a “National Day of Action,” coinciding with dozens of other anti-ICE protests across the country. Protests began in Biddeford in the hours after the shooting on Monday and have continued each day across Maine since.

Holding signs calling for the abolition of ICE, the ousting of Republican Sen. Susan Collins from the U.S. Senate and justice for Guerrero, the protestors joined in chants, shouting “No hate, no fear, immigrants are welcome here,” “ICE out” and “ICE pulled the trigger, but Collins gave the gun.”

“I’m outraged that our government is killing people in the streets,” said Dawn Piccolo, 65, of Old Orchard Beach. “That’s not the way this country is supposed to be.”

Alex Briggs, who lives in Cumberland County, flew a large anti-facist flag on a 10-foot pole. He said he believes that moderate Democrats are not doing enough to fight what he sees as the creeping sense of facism in the United States.

“We need to be forceful to meet this moment,” Briggs said.

Advertisement

Guerrero’s killing sent shockwaves across the country and around the world. His death has heightened the anxiety many in Maine’s immigrant communities have felt since January, when ICE initiated a weeklong “enhanced enforcement” operation in the state and detained more than 200 people.

ICE had ramped up its presence in Maine and around the country more recently in the weeks leading up to Guerrero’s killing. The agency has arrested more people in the first three weeks of July than any other month in President Donald Trump’s second term, according to Department of Homeland Security data shared with Congress and published by The Washington Post.

An average of two Mainers a day have been arrested by ICE since May, according to the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition and data from the organization’s ICE activity hotline.

The crowd at Monument Square gathered to hear a handful of community protesters speak against ICE.

“The people deserve to hear the truth. We demand that the attorney general update this community on a regular basis about this investigation and the steps being taken,” said community organizer Faisal Khan, referring to Guerrero’s killing. “We can no longer just assume we will win. We want answers now.”

The alleged shooter is David Brouillette, a 37-year-old from Manchester whose family members allege has a history of domestic violence and mental health episodes. Two of his ex-wives have spoken out, saying they feared for their lives while they were married to him.

Another speaker, Sophie Garner, told the crowd that she lives a few blocks away from where Guerrero was killed.

“When things like this happen in our own backyards, it is beyond hard to grapple with,” Garner said. “The illusion that our communities are safe has been shattered long ago.”

The speakers’ statements were met with roars of applause and cheering.

title: Times Opinion: Fund families, not cruel crackdowns | Chattanooga Times Free Press
description:
It's just that Trump wants to spend it on other things, like funding U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol.
American families are grappling with a cost of living crisis; many are struggling to cover rent, groceries, electric bills and healthcare.
Yet rather than helping working people, Republicans have authorized a staggering $240 billion for the systematic separation of families and disruption of communities.
The $240 billion is paid for by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's severe cuts to Medicaid and SNAP.
Congress should claw back the $240 billion it has allocated for mass deportations and detention and not give a dollar more.
text:
President Donald Trump and other Republicans like to say the United States does not have money for programs that address the needs of ordinary citizens.

"It's not possible for us to take care of day care, Medicaid, Medicare, all these individual things," Trump said recently, saying the nation had more important things to do, like "fighting wars."

But the nation has plenty of money for such programs. It's just that Trump wants to spend it on other things, like funding U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol.

In a largely party-line vote this June, Congress granted the Trump administration another $70 billion for ICE and others to conduct mass deportations and detention. This colossal increase came less than a year after the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which allocated an unprecedented $170 billion through 2029 for his cruel immigration crackdown.

American families are grappling with a cost of living crisis; many are struggling to cover rent, groceries, electric bills and healthcare. Yet rather than helping working people, Republicans have authorized a staggering $240 billion for the systematic separation of families and disruption of communities.

This equates to eight years of funding for ICE and Border Patrol. It is a sum greater than the gross domestic product of 161 nations.

Meanwhile, public approval for immigration enforcement agencies has plummeted as Americans have watched ICE agents invade cities, separate families and brutalize citizens and non-citizens alike. We've seen people locked up in inhumane detention centers, where record numbers of people have died in custody. Others have been deported to countries they've never before set foot in, often without due process.

Worse still, the money funding these abuses comes directly out of programs that actually help families. The $240 billion is paid for by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's severe cuts to Medicaid and SNAP.

This law is expected to strip health insurance from an estimated 16 million people by 2034. At least 4 million people have lost access to SNAP assistance since the bill was enacted in July 2025. Millions more are likely to lose benefits in the near future as the program shifts more costs to the states, another first under the law.

Instead of funding the mass deportation machine, the National Priorities Project at the Institute for Policy Studies, where I work, has found better ways to put that $240 billion to use.

With the amount we're now spending on rogue immigration agencies, we could instead fully restore this year's cuts to SNAP ($18.6 billion) and Medicaid ($91 billion) from the One Big Beautiful Bill; provide medical care for more than 1 million veterans through 2029 ($71.6 billion); establish universal preschool for kids across the U.S. ($35 billion); and make school lunches free for all 30 million children served through the National School Lunch Program ($6.38 billion).

We could do all that as well as power more than 10 million households with solar energy through 2029 ($17 billion), investing in long-term renewable energy while American families grapple with rising fossil fuel costs.

Our government needs to put families first. We can't let ICE and Border Patrol continue to harm our communities while the rest of us struggle to pay our bills and afford groceries.

Yet, astonishingly, House Republicans are asking for another $30 billion for immigration enforcement in fiscal year 2027. They seem determined to keep moving in the wrong direction.

Congress should claw back the $240 billion it has allocated for mass deportations and detention and not give a dollar more.

Alliyah Lusuegro is the outreach coordinator for the National Priorities Project at the Institute for Policy Studies.

text:
White House border czar Tom Homan said on Sunday, "I think body cameras are the way to go," after fatal shootings by federal officers in Texas and Maine earlier this month.

"I think body cameras let the American people know what that officer sees when he takes that action," Homan said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

On July 7, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed a Mexican national in Houston who had lived in the U.S. for decades. Days later, an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine. In both cases, the immigration personnel involved in the shootings were not wearing body cameras.

Homan said Sunday that "you can have a cellphone camera from a witness on the side, you can have, you know, city cameras or whatever. But I want the American people to see what that officer sees when he makes the decision and takes an action."

"I think the American people need to see what that officer sees and hears," Homan added. "I think it's important."

Homan has previously advocated for body cameras. And last week, the Department of Homeland Security announced that every Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrest team will have at least one officer equipped with a camera going forward. DHS said shortly after the Houston shooting that body cameras had been deployed to more than half of ICE's field offices, with the remaining offices set to receive them within 60 days.

The body cameras issue was part of negotiations between Senate Democrats and Republicans during a shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year. At the time, Democrats refused to fund the department as they sought reforms to the administration's immigration enforcement operation following two deadly shootings by federal agents in Minneapolis in January.

During the negotiations over immigration enforcement, the Trump administration signaled openness to expanding the use of body cameras. But negotiations ultimately fell apart. Democrats eventually opted to approve funding for the rest of the department in April, which included $20 million for body cameras, while Republicans later approved a roughly $70 billion package unilaterally to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol through the end of the Trump administration.

Homan on Sunday pointed to the DHS shutdown, claiming, "Everybody in ICE would have a camera now if the government wasn't shut down by Democratic members of Congress."

"There was money in that bill that they held up," he said. "But because the government shut down, we're behind on that."

Democratic lawmakers have criticized DHS's slow rollout of body cameras, given the funding approved in April, along with the "big, beautiful bill" passed last year. But Homan said the $20 million the department received earlier this year "wasn't enough."

"It didn't fund everything, but now we have the funding after reconciliation," Homan said, referring to the $70 billion package passed in June. "The cameras have been purchased, right now they're training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide."

The shootings in Texas and Maine have drawn renewed scrutiny on ICE's practices. Homan said "we got to let the investigations play out," but he noted that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin "took some action in concern of the safety of the agents and how we do operations" with a pause on vehicle stops. President Trump overturned that suspension on Wednesday. Both men were shot during attempted vehicle stops, and DHS has acknowledged that they were not the intended targets of the immigration operations.

Homan said more broadly, he's concerned about rhetoric, pointing to statements, including from members of Congress, encouraging people to resist Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He said "I actually think that emboldens some people to say, 'I'm not going to comply with ICE.'"

"And I think no matter what people think of ICE, no matter what you think of immigration law, you should always comply with law enforcement," Homan said.

Homan said even unmarked law enforcement vehicles are equipped with emergency lights and sirens, along with an insignia worn by officers, that he argued would make clear that they're law enforcement. In the Maine and Texas cases, Homan said he didn't know whether those lights were used.

"I'm saying our vehicles are equipped with emergency lights," Homan said. "If they didn't activate the lights, then there's an issue there."

text:
By December, federal immigration authorities had loaded more than 6,000 Nicaraguans on dozens of flights bound for their home country during the first year of the Trump administration.

Delvin Rodriguez was not among them. But it wasn’t for lack of trying: In late October, a month after he was arrested during a traffic stop on his way to a construction site near Dillon, the 39-year-old Colorado resident, who did not have permanent legal status, agreed to leave the country. Two of his sisters recalled that Rodriguez had spoken with a lawyer, who told him fighting his case would be expensive and likely unsuccessful, in part because he’d been arrested by immigration authorities when he first entered the country in 2018.

At first, through phone calls from the detention center in Aurora, he’d assured his sisters that he was only on vacation. After he met the lawyer and decided to stop fighting his removal, he was calm, his family remembered.

“I said that it was OK. I respected his decision,” remembered one sister. Both spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retaliation by ICE. “Everything’s in God’s hands. Either way, he was going home.”

But Rodriguez did not go home. Before Christmas — more than two months after he first entered the detention system — he was dead in Mississippi, one of a growing number of immigrant detainees who’ve died in custody over the past 18 months.

Rodriguez was the first person arrested in Colorado to die in immigration custody in eight years, according to a review of the agency’s official releases, and he was the 32nd immigrant to die in federal custody under President Donald Trump’s second administration. In the seven months since his death, that total has increased to 55.

His death was ruled a suicide by a Mississippi medical examiner, according to an autopsy report obtained through a public records request. At least nine other detainees have died by suicide since January 2025, amid the federal government’s efforts to rapidly increase arrests while gutting the independent agencies charged with scrutinizing the country’s rapidly expanding immigrant detention network.

In the months since, his family and a Colorado advocacy group have pressed for answers on the circumstances of his death and why he was still detained. With the help of a U.S. senator, some details have emerged only in recent days.

After his arrest, Rodriguez spent 66 days in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Aurora detention facility, according to ICE detention records analyzed by The Denver Post. He was briefly logged at a holding room in Arizona before moving again, on Dec. 1, to one of the nation’s largest detention facilities, housed in a private prison in Mississippi.

When he arrived, Rodriguez called his sisters. He told them he had not eaten much because there wasn’t enough food, they recalled. He was anxious about why he hadn’t left the country yet.

Two days later, he was isolated in an open-door cell after he exhibited behavior that “concerned” staff at the Adams County Correctional Center in Mississippi, said Alex Sánchez of Voces Unidas, an advocacy group working with Rodriguez’s family. Sánchez was present for a briefing about Rodriguez’s case last week by U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet’s office. The cell’s open door would allow staff members to monitor him “at all times,” and Sánchez said the setting sounded akin to suicide watch.

His sisters remembered talking to Rodriguez on the phone. They said he still seemed calm.

On Dec. 4, the day after he was moved to the cell, Rodriguez was found unresponsive around 4:15 p.m. On-site staff gave him CPR, and paramedics arrived at roughly 4:40 p.m., according to statements from ICE and CoreCivic, the company that operates the prison. He spent the next 10 days on life support in a nearby hospital, where he died on Dec. 14.

Officials from ICE and from CoreCivic have released little additional information about his case.

“Where was the staff (who) were in charge? Were there cameras, what truly happened?” his sister said earlier this year in an interview with The Post, before the family was provided details about his placement in a special cell. She spoke Spanish and communicated through an interpreter. “We want a test of justice for him.”

It’s unclear when the center’s staff members last checked on Rodriguez before he was found unresponsive, or why he was able to attempt suicide in a setting that seemed designed to prevent it.

“It was the middle of the day, so where were they?” Sánchez said of the staff members who were supposed to monitor Rodriguez. “How does it happen in the middle of the day, especially when it sounds like staff did some kind of intervention (the day before)?”

According to ICE’s detention standards, detainees at risk of suicide “may” be placed in a “suicide-resistant cell with constant (one-to-one) monitoring” that must be documented every 15 minutes. The cell must be free of “objects or structural elements that could facilitate a suicide attempt.”

ICE denied a records request seeking documents about Rodriguez’s case, citing an ongoing law enforcement investigation. An unnamed agency representative did not respond when asked about the investigation, instead referring The Post to ICE’s December news release about Rodriguez’s death.

Suicides in detention centers face scrutiny

In a May investigation into detainee suicides, the Associated Press found that ICE detention centers have repeatedly fallen short in ways that violate ICE’s own standards. An examination of the 10 suicide deaths found the detainees died in facilities that had ignored signs of distress, delayed mental health treatment and failed to monitor detainees who were already deemed at risk.

They also permitted detainees to have access to materials that could be used for self-harm, the AP found. Rodriguez used items in his cell to hang himself, according to the autopsy report, an ICE statement and information gleaned by Sánchez during the briefing by Bennet’s office. Several other detainee deaths have involved similar means, according to a Post review of ICE fatality reports.

“Someone should not be able to kill themselves in a detention center or a prison,” William Lopez, a public health professor at the University of Michigan who studies incarceration and deportation, told The Post. “… One should not be able to kill someone else in one of these facilities; one should not be able to harm someone else. The fact that it’s been happening, again, points to ineptitude.”

When ICE announced Rodriguez’s death, the agency said he had received a mental health screening two days before he was found in his cell and that he was cleared for the general population. The report does not mention that staff members were concerned about his behavior or that they had placed him in a cell for closer monitoring.

Last week, Rodriguez’s family learned more about the circumstances surrounding his death from Bennet’s office, which had been briefed by officials from the Department of Homeland Security.

In a statement, Bennet spokeswoman Sophie Ulin said agency officials had explained “the timeline of events and outlined the procedures that were followed.”

ICE did not respond to questions about the briefing. In a March statement, ICE spokeswoman Angelina C. Vicknair said that all detainees are “provided comprehensive medical care from the moment they enter ICE custody … (including) a medical, dental, and mental health intake screening within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arrival at a facility, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.”

CoreCivic also did not respond when asked about the family’s briefing. In an April statement to The Post, spokesman Brian Todd said the incident had been thoroughly reviewed.

“We adhere to all applicable federal detention standards in our ICE-contracted facilities, including our Adams County Correctional Center,” he wrote. “Our immigration facilities are monitored very closely by our government partners at ICE, and they are required to undergo regular review and audit processes to ensure an appropriate standard of living and care for all detainees.”

As of April, the Mississippi facility was the second-largest ICE detention center in America by average daily population, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University. A federal audit released last summer said it had five mental health observation cells, 202 detention officers and six mental health providers for a facility capable of housing more than 2,100 detainees at a time.

Brandon Riches, an immigration attorney in Mississippi who previously conducted legal training for detainees in the facility, said the detention center was one of the nicer ones he’d been in. But it still felt like a “maximum-security prison.”

“Locks on the doors, push the button to get through, the whole nine yards,” he said.

Still, like many other detention centers, the facility has a checkered history.

In May, federal inspectors found that the facility had failed to properly review and document staff members’ use of force.

In 2012, three years after Adams County opened its doors, immigrant detainees launched a deadly riot over the facility’s conditions. An affidavit by an FBI agent, first reported by the Jackson Free Press, said detainees rioted over “inadequate or substandard food, medical conditions and disrespectful staff members.” Hostages were taken, and one correctional officer was killed.

Nine years later, in 2021, the inspector general for the Department of Homeland Security found that a sick detainee died in the facility after staff failed to send the patient to the hospital. Federal inspectors also criticized the facility’s communication between detainees and staff, as well as its grievance standards.

‘He had been through a lot’

In his final conversations with his sisters, Rodriguez told them the facility was crowded and that he wasn’t receiving enough food.

He’d supported his sisters and mother since he began working at age 18. He’d served in the Nicaraguan military, then worked in construction in Costa Rica before traveling to the United States, where he applied for asylum.

“He had been through a lot before relocating to the U.S.,” said Karen McCarthy, an attorney who represented Rodriguez during his prior immigration proceedings. They also lived in the same neighborhood in Summit County. “He struck me as an honest person. I enjoyed getting to know him. He was always very cordial and polite, and somebody you wanted as a neighbor.”

When ICE announced Rodriguez’s death, the agency said he had been scheduled to fly home on Dec. 13 — the day before he was removed from life support.

The Mississippi prison to which he was moved is a short drive from a major airport in Alexandria, Louisiana. A sort of reverse Ellis Island, Alexandria is one of the primary departure points for deportation flights, particularly for those heading to Nicaragua, according to flight reports tracked by Human Rights First, a nonprofit group that defends immigrants’ and refugees’ rights. There were 10 flights to Managua, the country’s capital, in November, and nine more in December.

Why Rodriguez wasn’t on any of those flights is unclear.

Federal agencies have declined to provide specific information about his case, and he did not have a lawyer for most of his time in detention. His family said he had signed papers with ICE to stop contesting his removal. ICE records indicate his deportation order was signed Oct. 24.

Rodriguez told his sisters he was missing some sort of travel document, though his family had his passport. To maximize efficiency, ICE often keeps people from the same country detained until it can fill an entire flight, according to several immigration attorneys who spoke generally about ICE practices. Deportation timelines vary based on factors that are often opaque, those attorneys said.

“People don’t actually get deported rapidly all the time,” said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, a national advocacy group. “There are a lot of cases in which individuals can languish in detention for days, weeks, even months prior to deportation. That’s because the actual act of deportation itself requires coordination inside the government.”

Rodriguez’s missing travel document may have slowed his deportation, attorneys said. Hans Meyer, an immigration attorney in Denver, said Rodriguez may have had “horrifically bad luck, and he got disappeared into a horrible black hole.”

On the day that Rodriguez died, there were more than 68,400 people in immigration detention centers across the United States. That was an all-time high, according to the Guardian.

“That is just the reality of the system,” Reichlin-Melnick said. “People get caught in it and fall through the cracks and end up not being deported, even though they desperately are asking to be.”

Protesters packed the plaza at Seattle Central College, chanting and carrying signs. The gathering is part of more than 70 ICE OUT rallies expected to take place across the country over the weekend.

“If it can happen to them, it can happen to anyone. It can happen to us, even though we are American citizens,” Bobacilla said.

Participants told KIRO 7 they were tired of the violence and fear.

“There’s just a lot of injustice going on, especially for Hispanics,” Jose Vargas said. “And a lot of it doesn’t make sense.”

text:
An FBI agent arrived at a crime scene and saw something suspicious: tied plastic baggies containing unknown substances resembling illegal drugs.

He would need to laboratory test the items to be sure. To do that, he would also get a warrant.

The Houston incident, following one of the latest deadly shootings by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, mirrors countless routine police encounters that happen daily across the country as officers find suspected drug paraphernalia and seek court orders to seize and test it for illegal substances.

In this instance, however, the search warrant, shielded from public view when initially filed, was inexplicably unsealed and made public the next day. Justice Department veterans told CNN they can’t remember a time when information that could be critical to a case was made publicly available while a criminal investigation was still underway.

“This is absolutely abnormal,” said Elie Honig, CNN senior legal analyst and former federal prosecutor. “This raises all sorts of red flags and all sorts of questions about why they would unseal this now.”

The move quickly set off a firestorm, with immigration rights advocates accusing DOJ of trying to malign a dead man. And some legal experts are now questioning whether the department is playing politics in an unprecedented way with a high-profile criminal investigation.

‘It just smells of a smear campaign,’ an advocate says

The still-unidentified substances were allegedly found on the dashboard and floor of a van driven by Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Houston man ICE tried to pull over last week on suspicion of being in the country unlawfully. Importantly, he was not their original target. Instead, federal authorities said immigration officers were initially searching for undocumented migrants in another vehicle that resembled Salgado Araujo’s van when they initiated the traffic stop.

In a statement, which mirrors similar past statements issued by the Department of Homeland of Security during the Trump’s administration’s nationwide immigration enforcement surge, ICE said Salgado Araujo “rammed an ICE law enforcement vehicle, refused to follow multiple verbal commands, and weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over an ICE law enforcement officer” before an immigration officer shot and killed him in self-defense.

No video has surfaced depicting the moment of the shooting and none of the officers were wearing body cameras. Men who were riding in the van with Salgado Araujo and his brother, Victor, told attorney Hugo Balderas-Ibarra they did not attempt to ram officers, nor put the officers in danger.

Salgado Araujo also had no prior criminal record despite the Trump administration’s claims it is targeting the ‘worst of the worst.’

In an affidavit seeking to search the vehicle filed in federal court Tuesday, the FBI agent who responded to the incident wrote “the white in color crystal-like substances packaged in small clear plastic bags are consistent with how users of drugs package controlled substances for distribution, manufacturing, and possession,” adding it was “consistent with methamphetamine.”

As is normal in active, high-profile investigations, the federal court docket shows the search warrant was originally filed by DOJ under seal, shielding its contents from public view.

But, a day later, in a move many who served in law enforcement viewed as baffling, the warrant appeared to have been suddenly unsealed while the ongoing investigation into the incident was still underway. It was quickly picked up by the media, with articles and TV segments spotlighting the FBI’s suspicion that Salgado Araujo was transporting methamphetamine.

The US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the allegations in the warrant; why the warrant information was made public; and whether it was unsealed at the request of federal prosecutors.

Notably, attorney Ruby Powers representing Salgado Araujo’s family refuted the notion he was in possession of drugs, saying in a statement the family believed the plastic baggies actually contained “granulated salt, which is paired with lemon and water as a homemade electrolyte mix used by outdoor workers in extreme Texas heat, not methamphetamine or any other illicit substance.”

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, who has criticized federal authorities for not cooperating with his office’s investigation into the shooting, told CNN he also does not believe the substance the FBI found was drugs. The FBI has not commented on whether testing of the items has been completed.

In addition to criticizing the unsealing of the search warrant in the case, Teare told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Friday that he did not believe the FBI fully processed the van for evidence. That might include records from the vehicle’s computer system indicating its speed, steering, and braking, he said, as well as swabbing the exterior for DNA that may prove immigration officers were in physical contact with the van.

“All they were looking for were baggies that were in open sight, and the only thing that I can think they did it for was to smear a good man’s name,” he said.

The president of the LULAC Adelante PAC, a political group that supports Latino voter participation and candidates, accused federal investigators of trying to “change the public discourse and prejudice a jury in Harris County.”

“It just smells of a smear campaign and a cover up,” Domingo Garcia said Wednesday.

‘No reason to unseal it now,’ says DOJ veteran

“No prosecutor would ever unseal a warrant at this phase of an investigation under any ordinary circumstances,” said Honig, who served in the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

He said warrants are typically only unsealed after a case has been indicted by a federal grand jury and federal prosecutors begin sharing evidence with the defense as required.

“There is no reason to unseal it now,” Honig said. “All you do is risk revealing information about your investigation you don’t want revealed. You could compromise your investigation, compromise witnesses, and undermine your own case.”

If the unusual step to unseal the search warrant was indeed meant to sully the reputation of Salgado Araujo and his passengers, it may have worked. Social media was ablaze with demeaning comments. Some, however, directed their skepticism and hostility towards ICE and the FBI, openly questioning why they would think someone would actually drive around with methamphetamine clearly visible on their dashboard.

One notable aspect of this apparent subplot is how little the presence of drugs, if eventually verified by FBI testing, would likely factor at all into the DHS Office of Inspector General’s ongoing investigation of the ICE officer’s decision to use deadly force. To date, DHS has not indicated the ICE officers who stopped Salgado Araujo had any knowledge of drugs possibly being inside the vehicle at the time of the fatal shooting.

It does remain to be seen whether any allegations of drug possession may be used in possible deportation proceedings for the passengers who were riding with him. The DA in Houston has requested they be afforded special visas while multiple investigations remain underway, calling the men witnesses to alleged crimes.

In a statement Thursday that did not address any of the questions raised about the unsealing of the search warrant in the case, Trump-appointed US Attorney Aaron Reitz, who took office this month after previously working for Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX) and in Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office, insisted he is not “drawing any final conclusions while the investigation is ongoing.”

Reitz said federal authorities “are doing everything we can to seek the truth and do the right thing. In the meantime, I encourage the public to give the FBI and DHS the opportunity to investigate.”
